1.title: A friendship that changed course
1.brief: Write a reflective piece about a friendship that changed over time — one that grew stronger, faded or ended. Explain how you met, what kept you together and what changed. Use the phrasal verbs of the unit naturally and show how both of you felt at key moments.
criteria: Six phrasal verbs from the unit (e.g. hit it off, fall out, drift apart, make up), used with the correct particle and object position.
Three gerund constructions and three infinitive constructions, including one perfect infinitive (to have known) and one passive gerund (being ignored).
A clear arc: beginning, turning point and present reflection, with one sentence that expresses polite disagreement or regret.

2.title: Do clothes make the person?
2.brief: Write an opinion essay answering the question “Do the clothes we wear say more about us than our words do?” Consider first impressions at work, social media and personal identity, and give your own conclusion.
criteria: Three cleft sentences with what (What surprises me is…, What people notice first is…).
Five different verb patterns: verb + -ing, verb + to-infinitive, verb + object + infinitive, make/let + object + base form, and a verb that changes meaning (stop, remember, try).
A balanced argument: one paragraph for, one against, and a conclusion that takes a clear position.

3.title: A breakthrough worth the hype?
3.brief: Write an article for a science magazine about a recent technology (AI tutors, gene editing, electric planes…). Describe how it works in simple terms, who benefits, the risks, and whether the hype is justified.
criteria: Correct use of articles with generic and specific nouns (Technology changes… / The technology I describe…), including one zero-article plural and one uncountable noun.
Four -ing clauses to add information or show cause (Having tested the app, researchers… / Using less energy, the device…).
Five words from the unit (breakthrough, cutting-edge, roll out, game-changer…) and a headline plus a one-line standfirst.

4.title: The hoax that fooled everyone
4.brief: Write a news-style report about a famous hoax, rumour or superstition (real or invented). Explain what was claimed, how people reacted, what experts said and how the truth came out.
criteria: Four reporting verbs with different patterns (claim, deny + -ing, warn + object + to, insist that).
Three passive reporting structures (It is believed that…, The photo was said to have been…, He is thought to be…).
Neutral journalistic tone: no personal opinions until a final sentence that evaluates how gullible the public was.

5.title: Review: a series worth binge-watching
5.brief: Write a review of a film or TV series for a website aimed at young adults. Summarise the premise without spoilers, comment on acting, plot twists and pacing, and say who should watch it.
criteria: Four sentence adverbs to show your attitude (Admittedly, Surprisingly, Ultimately, Frankly), each at the start of a sentence with a comma.
Two such…that and two so…that sentences (The ending was so predictable that…; It has such a gripping plot that…).
A recommendation with a star rating and at least five words from the unit (plot twist, spoiler, blockbuster, binge-watch…).

6.title: What makes a song last?
6.brief: Write an essay or blog post about why some songs become classics while others are one-hit wonders. Use examples from artists you know and describe how your own listening habits have changed over the years.
criteria: Three double comparatives (The more you hear it, the catchier it becomes).
Three sentences with will or would for habits and typical behaviour (My dad would play vinyl every Sunday; Fans will queue for hours).
Concrete examples of at least two artists and five words from the unit (catchy, go viral, one-hit wonder, tone-deaf…).

7.title: Then and now: a letter across generations
7.brief: Write a letter to a grandparent or older relative comparing your life at your age with theirs: work, technology, family and freedom. Be respectful, include gentle humour and end with a question for them.
criteria: Relative clauses where you decide correctly when the pronoun can be omitted (the town I grew up in) and when it is required (the people who raised me).
Three comparisons with as if / as though / the way / like (It feels as if life moves faster now; nobody writes letters the way you did).
An informal but polished letter format (greeting, paragraphs, sign-off) and four words from the unit (upbringing, generation gap, settle down, nostalgia).

8.title: A proposal to change shopping habits
8.brief: You are on your college or company's sustainability committee. Write a proposal to reduce impulse buying and waste among students or staff, with concrete measures, costs and expected results.
criteria: Three subjunctive structures (We recommend that every student be…; It is essential that the shop not offer…; I propose that the committee review…).
Correct placement of direct and indirect objects, including phrasal verbs and pronouns (give it to them, hand them out, offer students a discount).
Proposal format: title, introduction, two or three headed sections and a conclusion; five words from the unit (impulse buy, brand loyalty, bargain, haggle…).

9.title: Should zoos still exist?
9.brief: Write a discursive essay on whether zoos help or harm animals today. Discuss conservation, education, animal welfare and alternatives such as sanctuaries and wildlife reserves.
criteria: Three clauses with whenever / wherever and their contrast with when / where (Wherever habitats disappear, … / the park where I volunteered).
Two noun clauses with whoever / whatever (Whoever visits a zoo… ; whatever the benefits are…).
Formal discursive structure with linking words of contrast and concession and five words from the unit (endangered, habitat, poach, conservation…).

10.title: My relationship with English
10.brief: Write a personal essay about learning English: the moments you felt fluent, the mistakes that taught you most, how dialects and slang challenge you, and what you would tell a beginner.
criteria: Five passives in different forms, including one passive with a modal and one with get (I was never taught…, It should be learned…, I got corrected).
Correct subject-verb agreement with quantifiers (Most of my classmates are…, None of the advice was…, A number of words have…).
Personal anecdotes plus one piece of advice; five words from the unit (fluent, dialect, slang, mother tongue…).

11.title: A person I genuinely admire
11.brief: Write a profile of a role model — famous or from your own life — for a website celebrating exceptional people. Describe their background, the obstacles they overcame and the values that make them stand out.
criteria: Five compound adjectives (hard-working, open-minded, well-respected, world-famous, long-lasting).
Two superlative compound adjectives (the best-known, the most hard-working).
A clear structure: hook, background, turning point, legacy; four words from the unit (role model, look up to, determined, resilient…).

12.title: A pitch for your startup idea
12.brief: Write a short business plan or pitch email to an investor for a startup you would like to create. Explain the problem, your solution, the market, how you will break even and what you need from the investor.
12.length: email or plan with headings · about 320 words
criteria: Three conditionals with inversion (Should you decide to invest…, Were the market to grow…, Had we launched earlier…).
Four adverb clauses of condition (provided that, as long as, unless, in case, even if).
Persuasive, professional tone and five words from the unit (startup, break even, close a deal, think outside the box…).
